thread.title: Jabil deal could put GoPro technology into more devices

author: Margie Manning
title: Jabil deal could put GoPro technology into more devices
text: – Finance Editor, Tampa Bay Business Journal Mar 22, 2018, 2:54pm EDT Camera lenses and images sensors from GoPro could find new uses in everything from home automation to self-driving cars, as part of a new agreement between the camera maker and Jabil Inc. Jabil (NYSE: JBL), an electronics services provider headquartered in St. Petersburg, and San Mateo, California-based GoPro (NASDAQ: GPRO) signed a global, multiyear technology and equipment license that lets Jabil incorporate GoPro technology into GoPro-approved third-party products and solutions. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed in a press release . Irv Stein , vice president of Jabil Optics, said Jabil would pay a licensing fee to GoPro when the company's technology is used for other products. The new deal also brings a cool factor to Jabil, a technology industry leader that is under the radar for most consumers. The company was launched 52 years ago at the founder’s kitchen table and has grown to become the second-largest public company in the Tampa Bay area, providing an inspiration for local startups. Jabil’s name, however, is not widely known because the company designs and manufactures products for other firms, including Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Cisco Systems (NASDAQ: CSCO), Hewlett-Packard (NYSE: HPQ) and others. While Apple historically has been Jabil’s biggest customer, Jabil’s cash flows and earnings are becoming more diversified and less dependent on any single product or product family, CEO Mark Mondello said during the company’s March 12 conference call with analysts. Jabil and GoPro have worked together for about four years, including on the launch of GoPro's HERO4 camera, Stein said. "Previously we only worked on GoPro products for them and held the intellectual property propriety for them," Stein said. "This allows us to leverage all that work into a number of markets and offer solutions via the licensing agreement to robotics, smart home, fire and police, and optics applications, such as cameras on bodies and conference centers." The wide field of view in the GoPro technology is similar to cameras used in the automotive market, Stein said. “Imagine a world where video conferencing, robotics and even self-driving cars are powered by GoPro’s camera lenses and image sensors,” Sandor Barna, GoPro’s chief technology officer, said in the release. “Together, GoPro and Jabil can make this a reality.” The deal allows Jabil's customers to leverage the GoPro technology at a reduced cost without having to go through the development themselves, Stein said. "It lowers the cost basis for them to get the product to market and offers innovative solutions they can apply in their marketplace more quickly." Nick Woodman , CEO of GoPro, hinted at the deal last month on Bloomberg TV, when he talked about new revenue streams for company, Silicon Valley Business Journal reported . “My job as CEO of GoPro is to look for opportunities to realize our vision and to create as big an opportunity for investors as possible. If that’s as a standalone, independent company that’s terrific, but if we can achieve that more easily and quickly with a partner, we would jump at the chance to look at the opportunity,” Woodman said. While Jabil has shown strong market performance, with its stock up more than 10 percent year to date, GoPro’s stock has fallen about 35 percent since Jan. 2. News broke in early January that the company was potentially looking for a buyer, exiting the drone business and laying off 20 percent of its workforce, Silicon Valley Business Journal said . – Finance Editor, Tampa Bay Business Journal Mar 22, 2018, 2:54pm EDT Related Content
